question: Synthesize what the corpus says about self-repair in code generation: describe the repair workflow, explain how LiveCodeBench evaluates related capabilities, and explain why counterfeit-samples work recommends caution with self-repair or model-based reranking.
answer:
The corpus presents self-repair as a multi-stage loop rather than “just” code generation.

### 1) Repair workflow
One paper defines self-repair as four stages: **code generation, code execution, feedback generation, and code repair**. A model first generates multiple code samples, the samples are executed against a test bed, failing programs produce error messages, a feedback model turns those error messages into a more detailed explanation, and then the code model uses that feedback to produce a repaired program [Source 7]. The paper also notes that, in practice, feedback generation and repair can sometimes be done in a single interaction, but it is still useful to think of them as separate steps [Source 5]. Another source summarizes the same “typical workflow” as sampling code, running unit tests, feeding the faulty program plus error message to a feedback model, and then repairing the code [Source 3].

### 2) How LiveCodeBench evaluates related capabilities
The available context says LiveCodeBench aims for a **holistic evaluation** of code LLMs using **four scenarios**: **code generation, self-repair, code execution, and test output prediction** [Source 12]. The motivation is that standard code generation alone captures only one dimension of capability, while these other scenarios correspond to useful components in code-LLM workflows and can be evaluated with clear automated metrics [Source 12].  
The corpus also mentions that LiveCodeBench’s execution scenario is inspired by CRUXEval [Source 6], but the retrieved documents do not provide more detail on the exact self-repair scoring procedure or benchmark protocol.

### 3) Why the counterfeit-samples work urges caution
The counterfeit-samples paper argues that counterfeits can be **adversarial to the model**: models often struggle to assess their correctness, reason about their execution as if they were correct programs, and repair them at a **low rate** [Source 2]. It also finds an **inconsistency between generation and understanding capabilities**: counterfeit samples from easier problems are not much easier to assess, execute, or repair [Source 2]. Because many downstream methods rely on a model using feedback to improve itself, the authors recommend **exercising caution** with schemes such as **self-repair and model-based reranking**, especially **when no external feedback is incorporated** [Source 2, Source 4].

A related self-repair paper makes a similar practical caution: **self-repair is not a silver bullet**, because once repair cost is counted, i.i.d. sampling can sometimes match or outperform repair, especially under small compute budgets [Source 8]. It also suggests that self-repair is bottlenecked by the model’s ability to provide feedback on its own code [Source 9].

So, taken together: self-repair uses a generate–execute–explain–repair loop; LiveCodeBench evaluates self-repair alongside generation, execution, and test-output prediction; and the counterfeit-samples results warn that models often cannot reliably understand or fix their own flawed outputs, so self-repair and reranking should be used carefully, particularly without external signals [Source 7, Source 12, Source 2, Source 4].

typical workflow. First, a program is sampled from a code generation model; this program is then run
on a suite of unit tests provided as part of the specification; if the program fails any test, then the error
message and the faulty program are given to a feedback generation model, which outputs a short
explanation of why the code failed; finally, the feedback is passed to a repair model, which generates
a fixed version of the program.1 On the surface, this is a very attractive idea. It allows the system to
overcome mistakes caused by unfortunate samples during decoding; easily incorporates feedback
during the repair phase from symbolic systems such as compilers, static analysis tools, and execution
engines; and mimics the trial-and-error way in which human software engineers write code.
However, it is important to remember that self-repair requires more invocations of the model, thus

Large language models have shown remarkable aptitude in code generation, but
still struggle to perform complex tasks. Self-repair—in which the model debugs
and repairs its own code—has recently become a popular way to boost performance

ability to perform self-repair on problems taken from HumanEval and APPS. We
find that when the cost of carrying out repair is taken into account, performance
gains are often modest, vary a lot between subsets of the data, and are sometimes
not present at all. We hypothesize that this is because self-repair is bottlenecked by

Contemporary work on LLM self-repair. There is much contemporary work seeking to self-repair
with LLMs, both in code generation and beyond. We now highlight a few of these works which are
particularly close to ours; see Pan et al. (2023) for a more complete survey of recent work in this
quickly evolving field. Zhang et al. (2023) explore self-repair without natural language feedback
on APPS (Hendrycks et al., 2021) using both finetuned models and prompt-based self-repair with
Codex (Chen et al., 2021), InCoder (Fried et al., 2023), and CodeGen (Nijkamp et al., 2023). Notably,
their framework does not consider the cost associated with feedback and repair, which presents a
significantly different perspective. Similarly, Chen et al. (2023b) assess Codex’s ability to self-repair
across a variety of tasks, in a framework that closely resembles that which we study in this work.

Code capabilities of LLMS are evaluated and compared using natural language to code generation
tasks. However, this only captures one dimension of code-related capabilities. AlphaCodium (Ridnik
et al., 2024) developed an intricate LLM pipeline for solving competition coding problems. By
combining natural language reasoning, test case generation, code generation, and self-repair, they
achieve significant improvements over a naive direct code generation baseline, showcasing the
importance of these broader capabilities. Motivated by this, we propose a holistic evaluation of LLMS
using a suite of evaluation setups that capture a broader range of code-related capabilities.
Specifically, we evaluate code LLMS in four scenarios, namely code generation, self-repair, code
execution, and test output prediction. Our selection criterion was to pick settings that are useful
components in code LLM workflows and in addition, have clear and automated evaluation metrics.
